metadata.focus: Twelve month-balanced source-led P1 alternate upgrades: one per calendar month
metadata.notes: A source pair establishes anniversary event/date/location only; detailed numerical claims, measurement metadata, dependencies, visual assets and rights remain unchecked. All 12 former NCEI segment leads preserved with original IDs and source URLs.

alternate_reviews.title: Chicago plunges to −16°F during the January 2014 Arctic outbreak
alternate_reviews.secondary_publisher: National Weather Service Chicago climate archive
alternate_reviews.verified_core_fact: Chicago recorded a minimum temperature of −16°F on January 6, 2014, at the heart of a multiday Arctic outbreak.
alternate_reviews.source_independence_assessment: Two NWS Chicago narratives reference the same official observing network; this is cross-document chronology, not independent thermometry.
alternate_reviews.unverified_claims: The -16°F is actual air temperature, not wind chill; distinguish the morning record from the daytime high, and January 6 from the Jan 5–7 outbreak.
alternate_reviews.graphic_concept: Original Chicago daily temperature time series against climate normals and an annotated Jan 6 minimum.

alternate_reviews.title: The Groundhog Day blizzard slams Chicago with thundersnow
alternate_reviews.verified_core_fact: A major blizzard intensified across Chicago on February 1, 2011, with thundersnow reported that night; the storm continued into February 2.
alternate_reviews.source_independence_assessment: NWS reconstructs radar and official snowfall; contemporary reporting documents local disruption, but repeats NWS storm figures.
alternate_reviews.unverified_claims: Storm-total accumulations include Jan 31–Feb 2; do not label the full 21.2-inch historical total as Feb 1 alone or imply a Feb 1 final snowfall record without corrections.
alternate_reviews.graphic_concept: Original hourly radar/pressure-and-snowfall timeline with Feb 1 overnight thundersnow.

alternate_reviews.title: Severe Mount Fuji lee-wave turbulence destroys BOAC Flight 911
alternate_reviews.location: Mount Fuji and Gotemba, Honshu, Japan
alternate_reviews.verified_core_fact: BOAC Flight 911 broke up near Mount Fuji on March 5, 1966, after encountering extraordinarily severe clear-air turbulence associated with lee waves.
alternate_reviews.source_independence_assessment: Retrospective aviation-safety summaries ultimately draw on the same Japanese accident investigation; not independent meteorological instruments.
alternate_reviews.unverified_claims: An aviation accident, not a weather-station measurement. Confirm 14:15 Japan local timestamp and exact investigator wording before specifying winds, load factors or causal chain.
alternate_reviews.graphic_concept: Original Mount Fuji terrain cross-section with conceptual lee-wave and aircraft path; explicitly schematic.

alternate_reviews.title: An April Fools’ blizzard buries eastern Massachusetts
alternate_reviews.location: Boston and Blue Hill, eastern Massachusetts
alternate_reviews.verified_core_fact: An extraordinary late-season snowstorm struck eastern Massachusetts from March 31 into April 1, 1997, with Blue Hill Observatory documenting its remarkable 24-hour snowfall.
alternate_reviews.source_independence_assessment: Blue Hill supplies station-specific historical records; Cornell independently discusses the regional meteorology but repeats official weather observations.
alternate_reviews.unverified_claims: Do not assign the storm's entire accumulation to April 1. Separate Boston and Blue Hill station values and historic record rankings as of the reporting year.
alternate_reviews.graphic_concept: Original storm-track and station-specific snowfall comparison with Mar 31–Apr 1 time band.

alternate_reviews.title: Record-breaking rainfall begins Nashville's historic May flood
alternate_reviews.verified_core_fact: Extreme rain began across Middle Tennessee on May 1, 2010, and continued May 2, initiating catastrophic flooding in the Nashville region.
alternate_reviews.source_independence_assessment: Different NWS offices describe nearby portions of a common synoptic event; underlying radar, gauges and impacts overlap.
alternate_reviews.unverified_claims: Many impacts occurred May 2–3; avoid assigning 48-hour rainfall, Cumberland River crest or regional death totals solely to May 1.
alternate_reviews.graphic_concept: Original rainfall accumulation clock and Nashville hydrograph with separate May 1–3 markers.

alternate_reviews.title: A powerful winter cold front batters Cape Town
alternate_reviews.location: Cape Town and Western Cape, South Africa
alternate_reviews.verified_core_fact: A powerful winter cold front brought severe winds and dangerous coastal conditions to Cape Town and the Western Cape around June 7, 2017.
alternate_reviews.source_independence_assessment: South African Weather Service supplied observing/forecast information; contemporaneous reporting repeats some forecasts and supplements with observed impacts.
alternate_reviews.unverified_claims: System crossed June 6–8. Do not conflate forecast wind ranges, measured gusts and offshore wave heights; the simultaneous Knysna fires have distinct causes/locations.
alternate_reviews.graphic_concept: Original surface-pressure/wind analysis with schematic frontal passage, dated June 7.

alternate_reviews.title: A stalled thunderstorm floods Vanguard, Saskatchewan
alternate_reviews.verified_core_fact: On July 3, 2000, intense, slow-moving convection produced extreme rain and flash flooding near Vanguard, Saskatchewan.
alternate_reviews.source_independence_assessment: Provincial and Canadian federal records date the flood; a hydrometeorological research paper analyzes storm rainfall but may use some same gauges/reconstructions.
alternate_reviews.unverified_claims: Government reporting says 333 mm in under 10 hours near Vanguard; a research study reports up to 375 mm in eight hours for its analyzed footprint. These need observation-site and period reconciliation. Rain continued into early July 4.
alternate_reviews.graphic_concept: Original storm-cell rainfall footprint schematic with clearly separated station 333-mm and area-maximum 375-mm observations.

alternate_reviews.title: Giant hailstones fall near Fort Walker, Virginia
alternate_reviews.location: Fort Walker area, Caroline County, Virginia
alternate_reviews.verified_core_fact: Storm chasers recovered hailstones as large as roughly 4.75 inches in diameter south of Fort Walker on August 7, 2023, as a severe storm crossed Virginia.
alternate_reviews.source_independence_assessment: NWS hail summary includes chaser-recovered measurements; media reporting may repeat those observations, not an independent instrument network.
alternate_reviews.unverified_claims: The maximum hail size is local to documented stones, not the whole storm track; verify specific verification procedure and any state-record superlatives, and do not reuse chaser photographs without license.
alternate_reviews.graphic_concept: Original hail-size scale graphic and dated geolocated storm track without copyrighted stone photos.

alternate_reviews.title: The 1935 Labor Day Hurricane strikes the Florida Keys
alternate_reviews.location: Upper and Middle Florida Keys, Florida
alternate_reviews.verified_core_fact: The exceptionally intense 1935 Labor Day Hurricane made landfall in the Florida Keys on September 2, 1935.
alternate_reviews.source_independence_assessment: NHC and AOML institutional histories rely on the same 1935 observations/reconstruction; two NOAA pages are not two independent pressure readings.
alternate_reviews.unverified_claims: Confirm time-zone and vessel-based pressure measurement metadata before quoting 892 hPa or precise landfall center. Fatality counts vary by scope and original archives.
alternate_reviews.graphic_concept: Original historical track, landfall timing and contemporary estimated central-pressure series.

alternate_reviews.title: Diablo winds drive the North Bay wildfires into Santa Rosa
alternate_reviews.location: Santa Rosa, Sonoma and Napa Counties, California
alternate_reviews.secondary_publisher: Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society study
alternate_reviews.primary_publisher: National Weather Service San Francisco Bay Area
alternate_reviews.verified_core_fact: From late October 8 into the early morning of October 9, 2017, extreme offshore downslope winds and very dry air accelerated multiple destructive North Bay wildfires.
alternate_reviews.source_independence_assessment: Peer-reviewed meteorological analysis uses RAWS/METAR observations and model diagnosis; NWS retrospective uses many of the same station records.
alternate_reviews.unverified_claims: Do not imply the fires first ignited on October 9: major ignitions began Sunday October 8 evening. Separate Tubbs/Nuns/Atlas/Pocket events and distinguish gust observations from inferred dynamics.
alternate_reviews.graphic_concept: Original synchronized RAWS wind/humidity time series and annotated spread corridor map.

alternate_reviews.title: Typhoon Vamco makes multiple landfalls in the Philippines
alternate_reviews.location: Polillo Islands and Quezon Province, Luzon, Philippines
alternate_reviews.primary_publisher: PAGASA (Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration)
alternate_reviews.verified_core_fact: Typhoon Vamco (Ulysses) crossed the eastern Philippines and made landfalls in Quezon Province on November 11, 2020, local time.
alternate_reviews.source_independence_assessment: PAGASA reconstructs the operational track and local landfalls, while NASA independently supplies satellite image context and can repeat PAGASA impact data.
alternate_reviews.unverified_claims: Multiple local landfalls and precise UTC/Philippine time distinctions matter; do not assign all later November 12 Manila flooding to the landfall instant, or mix preliminary and final wind estimates.
alternate_reviews.graphic_concept: Original storm-track map labeled by local and UTC landfall markers plus satellite-scene acquisition time.

alternate_reviews.title: A powerful early-December ice and snowstorm paralyzes Missouri
alternate_reviews.verified_core_fact: The November 30–December 1, 2006 winter storm produced widespread freezing precipitation and heavy snow affecting Missouri on December 1.
alternate_reviews.source_independence_assessment: NWS storm reconstruction uses instrument/surface observations; Missouri emergency managers document response impacts but some impact statements draw on NWS forecasts.
alternate_reviews.unverified_claims: Rain/ice began November 30 and impacts persisted into December. Separate freezing-rain glaze and sleet/snow zones; avoid treating a regional 2-day total as a Dec 1 station total.
alternate_reviews.graphic_concept: Original snow/ice placement map and regional daily precipitation-type timeline.
